title: OpenAI's new reasoning technique alarms AI safety experts
content:
OpenAI’s new Astra model will use a reasoning technique called “recurrent depth” that allows it to operate outside of the sequential thinking that characterizes most reasoning models, The Information reported on Tuesday. This technique, also called “opaque recurrence,” will likely make the model’s chain of thought more difficult to monitor — and that has AI safety experts rattled.
While Astra’s use of the technique is reportedly limited, its emergence has still raised significant concerns among AI safety experts.
“I am extremely concerned by the reporting that Astra uses opaque recurrence,” wrote Redwood CEO Buck Shlegeris in a post after the news broke. “I don’t know whether Astra is much less CoT monitorable than previous models. But if OpenAI pushes this technique further, they’ll have the option to massively increase the recurrence and totally destroys CoT monitorability.”
Longtime AI safety advocate Zvi Mowshowitz also weighed in and wrote that laws might be necessary to prevent a “race to the bottom” among AI labs.
“The technique is playing with fire, risking a taboo that OpenAI and Anthropic have fought to establish that we work hard to maintain Chain of Thought faithfulness and monitorability for as long as we can,” Mowshowitz wrote. “More intensive use of such techniques would probably damage monitorability.”
Under normal circumstances, a reasoning model’s chain of thought provides the sequential steps taken by the model as it attempts to solve a problem. While the representation is imperfect, it still serves as a valuable tool for monitoring misbehavior or misalignment. In the case of OpenAI’s recent rogue agent activity, chain-of-thought records were an important tool in teasing out why agents behaved the way they did.
In opaque recurrence, the model takes a less linear approach, processing the same query several times in a loop. The result leaves fewer legible traces, effectively side-stepping a conventional chain-of-thought record.
Crucially, Astra’s use of the technique appears to be limited. The model’s chain of thought is still expected to be legible, and the company pushed back against any suggestion that it would shift to “neuralese.” OpenAI has already announced plans for extensive chain-of-thought monitoring systems as part of its forward-looking safety plans.
In a post on X, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki emphasized the lab’s commitment to legible chains of thought. “OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models,” Pachocki wrote. “It’s a core goal of our current research program.
All AI models do some quantity of opaque reasoning, and few researchers take chain-of-thought logs as a direct representation of a model’s reasoning. Still, those caveats don’t dispel the concern that opaque recurrence may make AI reasoning harder to monitor, particularly as it grows in use across different models. In a follow-up report Wednesday morning, The Information reported that both Anthropic and Google DeepMind were already discussing the technique.
In a post responding to the news, Redwood Research chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt said opaque reasoning could easily scale faster than conventional chain-of-thought reasoning, effectively removing all reasoning from visible channels.
“My biggest concern is that a natural progression from here would involve scaling up the opaque reasoning to the point where the model reasons entirely or almost entirely in latent space,” Greenblatt wrote. “I hope it isn’t too late to avoid the most concerning architectures and that OpenAI will stop here.”

report.summary: OpenAI's Astra using recurrent depth reasoning could bypass chain-of-thought monitoring, alarming AI safety experts.
report.background: OpenAI's upcoming Astra model reportedly uses a reasoning technique called 'recurrent depth' — or 'opaque recurrence' — which is a departure from the sequential, legible chain-of-thought reasoning that has become standard in advanced AI models. Instead of producing visible step-by-step traces, the technique processes queries in loops, leaving fewer readable records for auditors. OpenAI says Astra's use is limited and that its chain-of-thought remains legible, but safety researchers warn that broader adoption could undermine 'CoT monitorability,' a key guardrail for detecting misalignment. Redwood Research's Buck Shlegeris and longtime advocate Zvi Mowshowitz both expressed alarm, with Mowshowitz suggesting new laws may be needed to prevent a race to the bottom among AI labs. Anthropic and Google DeepMind are already reportedly discussing the technique, amplifying concerns that opaque reasoning could become widespread before its risks are fully understood.
key_points: Recurrent depth, or opaque recurrence, allows an AI model to reason in loops rather than through a clear sequence of steps. This reduces the legible traces left behind, making it harder for researchers to inspect the model's internal problem-solving process and detect potential misbehavior.

AI safety experts argue that chain-of-thought records are critical safety tools. Redwood CEO Buck Shlegeris said he is 'extremely concerned,' while Zvi Mowshowitz warned that intense use of the technique risks damaging monitoring in the industry and may require new laws to avoid dangerous competition between labs.

OpenAI insists Astra's use of the technique is limited and does not abandon chain-of-thought. The company says its chain-of-thought remains legible, has promised monitoring systems, and its chief scientist stressed that preserving legible reasoning is a core research goal.

The technique is attracting industry-wide interest. The Information reports that both Anthropic and Google DeepMind are already discussing opaque recurrence, suggesting it may soon be considered by multiple leading labs, raising the stakes for industry-wide safety norms.

The biggest concern is escalation. Researchers warn that opaque reasoning could scale rapidly, eventually pushing models to reason almost entirely in hidden 'latent space,' which would strip away visible traces and make independent safety review nearly impossible.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this development highlights a growing trade-off between capability and oversight. If opaque recurrence becomes common, existing chain-of-thought monitoring, red-teaming, and post-hoc safety evaluations may become far less effective, forcing labs to develop new interpretability methods. Developers would face harder questions about how to debug or trust model behavior, especially after high-profile incident forensics relied on chain-of-thought records. Regular users may end up with more powerful but less explainable systems, which can undermine trust in areas like healthcare, law, and finance. It also increases pressure on regulators and frontier labs to establish enforceable transparency standards before 'race to the bottom' dynamics take hold.
report.tools: For follow-up, keep an eye on open-source interpretability libraries like TransformerLens and CircuitsVis for studying internal model mechanisms, plus LangSmith and Arize Phoenix for LLM trace and monitoring workflows. Redwood Research's public papers on chain-of-thought faithfulness, and OpenAI's own evals and CoT monitoring releases, are also worth tracking.
